title: Asking Needs-Based Questions
subtitle: How to ask the right questions to understand what a prospect actually needs
description: Master the language of discovery — how to ask open-ended questions that uncover real challenges, explore their impact, and help you understand what the prospect needs before you ever mention your product.
dialogueSubtitle: Riley is on a discovery call with Marcus, exploring the challenges his sales team is facing

vocabulary.definition: A specific problem or frustration that a customer experiences regularly — the thing that is making their work harder than it should be.
vocabulary.example: Before you pitch anything, you need to understand their pain points — what is actually slowing them down day to day.

vocabulary.definition: A point in a process that slows everything else down — where work gets stuck or piles up.
vocabulary.example: The bottleneck in their pipeline was the approval process — deals were getting stuck there for weeks before anyone followed up.

vocabulary.definition: The thing that matters most right now — what the team or business is focused on above everything else.
vocabulary.example: Understanding their priorities tells you which problems they are actually motivated to solve and which ones they can live with.

vocabulary.definition: A temporary solution someone uses because the proper fix is not in place yet — often a sign that a real problem exists.
vocabulary.example: When a prospect describes a workaround, that is a strong signal — it means the problem is real enough that they built something to manage it.

vocabulary.definition: To identify the root cause of a problem by asking the right questions — like a doctor figuring out what is wrong before prescribing anything.
vocabulary.example: A good discovery call is not about selling — it is about diagnosing. You are trying to understand the real problem, not just the surface one.

vocabulary.definition: To ask follow-up questions that go deeper into what the prospect has said — to get beyond the first answer.
vocabulary.example: When they say 'communication is an issue', probe — ask what that looks like in practice, who it affects, and how long it has been going on.

vocabulary.definition: To find out something the prospect has not volunteered — often a hidden problem or need that comes out through careful questioning.
vocabulary.example: The best discovery questions uncover problems the prospect did not even realise they wanted to talk about.

vocabulary.definition: The capacity a team has to take on new work, change, or initiative — if they have no bandwidth, even a great solution will not get implemented.
vocabulary.example: Before proposing anything, ask about bandwidth — if the team is already at capacity, timing becomes part of the conversation.

phrasalVerbs.phrase: WHAT DOES THAT LOOK LIKE IN PRACTICE
phrasalVerbs.definition: Ask the prospect to describe a problem concretely — move from a general statement to a real, specific example.
phrasalVerbs.example: You mention that handoffs between teams are a problem — what does that look like in practice? Can you walk me through a recent example?

phrasalVerbs.definition: Explore the impact of a challenge on the team, the process, or the business — moves the conversation from problem to consequence.
phrasalVerbs.example: How is that affecting the rest of the team? Are deals slipping because of it, or is it more of a morale issue at this point?

phrasalVerbs.phrase: WHAT HAVE YOU TRIED SO FAR
phrasalVerbs.definition: Find out what solutions the prospect has already attempted — avoids suggesting something they have already ruled out and shows you are listening.
phrasalVerbs.example: What have you tried so far to solve this? I want to make sure I understand what has worked and what has not before I suggest anything.

phrasalVerbs.phrase: IF YOU COULD CHANGE ONE THING
phrasalVerbs.definition: A focus question that helps the prospect identify their single biggest priority — useful when they have described multiple problems.
phrasalVerbs.example: If you could change one thing about how your team manages the pipeline right now, what would it be?

phrasalVerbs.definition: A future-state question that helps the prospect articulate what success means to them — gets them thinking about the outcome, not just the problem.
phrasalVerbs.example: What would good look like for you six months from now? If we solve this properly, what changes for your team?

phrasalVerbs.definition: Ask the prospect to describe a process, situation, or problem step by step — gives you a full picture rather than a summary.
phrasalVerbs.example: Walk me through what happens when a new lead comes in — from the moment it enters the system to the first call. I want to understand the full flow.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Marcus, thanks for making the time. Before I say anything about what we do, I'd love to understand your world a bit better. Can I ask you some questions first?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Of course — that's a refreshing way to start a call, actually.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Glad to hear it. So — walk me through how your team currently manages deals from first contact to close. I want to [[diagnose:to identify the root cause of a problem by asking the right questions]] before I suggest anything.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Sure. Leads come in from a few different channels — marketing, referrals, outbound. They go into the CRM, someone picks them up, and then honestly it gets a bit inconsistent from there.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: When you say inconsistent — what does that look like in practice? Is it the follow-up timing, the messaging, something else?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Mostly the follow-up. Some reps are on it within an hour, others take a day or two. It's become a real [[bottleneck:a point in a process that slows everything else down]] for us.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: How is that affecting your conversion rate? Are you seeing deals go cold because of the delay, or is it more of an internal visibility issue?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Both, honestly. We lose some deals, and I have no idea which ones until it's too late. The [[pain point:a specific problem or frustration a customer experiences regularly]] is really the lack of visibility.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Understood. What have you tried so far to address it? I want to know what has already been on the table before I go any further.

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: We built a [[workaround:a temporary solution used because the proper fix is not in place]] — a shared spreadsheet that reps are supposed to update daily. But it only works if everyone actually does it, which they don't.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: That makes sense — a manual [[workaround:a temporary solution used because the proper fix is not in place]] only works until it doesn't. If you could change one thing about how your pipeline works right now, what would it be?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: Honestly? Visibility. I want to know, at any point, exactly where every deal is and who is responsible for the next step.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: That's really helpful. Last question — what would good look like for you, say, six months from now? If we solve this properly, what changes for you and the team?

dialogue.speaker: Marcus
dialogue.text: I stop firefighting and start actually [[probe:to ask follow-up questions that go deeper]]ing into why deals are won or lost — rather than just trying to figure out where they went.

registerAwareness.example: 'Before I outline what we offer, I'd like to ask a few questions to make sure I understand your current situation. Is that all right? I want to make sure anything I propose is actually relevant to where you are right now.'
'OK, so — tell me what's actually going on. What's the thing that's driving you mad right now? I'd rather understand your world properly before I start talking about ours.'

'To help me prepare for our call, could you briefly describe: (1) your current process for managing pipeline, (2) the biggest challenge you are facing, and (3) what a successful outcome would look like for your team?'

'Following our conversation, I wanted to confirm my understanding of the key challenges you described: follow-up inconsistency, limited pipeline visibility, and a manual workaround that is not scaling. Please let me know if I have missed anything.'

Pain points: follow-up delay (1–2 days), no real-time visibility, spreadsheet workaround failing at scale. Priority: visibility above everything. No budget timeline given. Strong motivation — losing deals and doesn't know which ones.

registerTraps: ❌ Jumping to solutions before you have finished asking questions signals that you are selling, not listening — prospects notice immediately and disengage.
✅ Silence after a question is not awkward — it is the prospect thinking. Let them fill the pause. The best information often comes after a two-second gap.
🔁 Reflecting back what you heard ('So what you're saying is...') before asking the next question shows you were listening and gives the prospect a chance to correct or expand.

💡 'What have you tried so far?' is one of the most powerful questions in discovery — it tells you what they have already ruled out and shows you are not going to waste their time with suggestions they have already considered.

chooseResponse.instructions: Work in groups. Each situation calls for a discovery question. Choose the response that best uncovers what the prospect actually needs — not the one that sounds most polished. Discuss your reasoning before clicking.

items.customerLine: A prospect says: 'We have a lot of data but we're not really using it well.'
options: Say: 'That's very common — our platform actually solves that exact problem.'
Say: 'Interesting — what does that look like in practice? Is the data hard to access, or is it more that no one knows what to do with it once they have it?'
Say: 'How many data sources are you currently working with?'
items.explanation: B is correct. It probes the specific nature of the problem before suggesting anything. A jumps straight to a pitch — you haven't understood the problem yet. C asks a clarifying question but it's too narrow — it limits the conversation to a technical detail rather than understanding the real challenge.

items.customerLine: A prospect says they have tried three different tools in the last two years and none of them worked.
options: Say: 'I understand. Our tool is different because it is easier to implement.'
Say: 'What happened with each of them? I'd like to understand what didn't work before I say anything about what we do.'
Say: 'That sounds frustrating. Have you considered that the problem might not be the tools?'
items.explanation: B is correct. Understanding what went wrong with previous solutions is critical — it tells you what to avoid, what they have already ruled out, and what success would need to look like for them to trust a new solution. A makes a claim before you've earned the right to make it. C is presumptuous and risks putting the prospect on the defensive.

items.customerLine: A prospect says: 'Our biggest challenge right now is honestly just time. Everyone is stretched.'
options: Say: 'We can actually save your team time — that's one of the core things we help with.'
Say: 'That makes sense. How is that affecting the things that actually matter — are projects slipping, or is it more that the team is burning out?'
Say: 'Is it a resourcing issue or a process issue, do you think?'
items.explanation: B is correct. It explores the impact of the capacity problem — which is far more useful than a quick pivot to a solution or a binary diagnostic question. A jumps to a pitch before you've explored the problem. C is too closed — it forces a choice between two options when the real picture might be more nuanced.

items.customerLine: You have asked several questions and the prospect has described four or five different challenges. You need to find out which one matters most.
options: Say: 'OK — so it sounds like you have quite a lot going on. Where would you like to start?'
Say: 'If you could change one thing about how things work right now, what would make the biggest difference to you and the team?'
Say: 'Based on what you've told me, I think the biggest issue is the reporting — shall we focus on that?'
items.explanation: B is correct. It asks the prospect to identify their own priority rather than letting you choose for them — which is both more accurate and more persuasive, because they commit to it themselves. A is vague and hands control back without getting clarity. C makes an assumption about what matters most, which may be wrong — and even if it's right, it's more powerful when the prospect says it, not you.

profileMatch.instructions: Read the three prospect situations. As a group, decide which type of discovery question is the best first move for each. Match each prospect to the question type that fits their situation best, then click 'Check Matches'.

profiles.name: David
profiles.description: David has just taken over as Head of Sales. He inherited a team, a CRM, and a set of processes he didn't design. He has strong opinions about what isn't working but hasn't had time to dig into the root causes yet. He's energetic and wants to move fast.

profiles.name: Sonia
profiles.description: Sonia is the Operations Manager at a mid-size logistics company. She has described at least five different problems in the last three minutes — visibility, reporting, team communication, tool overload, and budget pressure. You are starting to lose the thread.

profiles.name: Tom
profiles.description: Tom mentions that his team has 'tried a few things' to fix their onboarding process but nothing has stuck. He seems slightly frustrated — maybe a bit cynical about new solutions. He hasn't said what he's tried yet.

options.label: Walk me through the current process
options.description: Use 'Walk me through...' to get a full picture before forming any opinions. When someone has inherited a situation they didn't design, a step-by-step walkthrough is the fastest way to identify where the real problems are — and avoids assuming you already know.

options.label: If you could change one thing
options.description: When a prospect has described too many problems, use 'If you could change one thing...' to help them identify their actual priority. Without this, you risk building a proposal around the wrong problem — or trying to solve everything at once.

options.label: What have you tried so far
options.description: When someone signals frustration with previous attempts, ask 'What have you tried so far?' first. It shows respect for what they've already done, tells you what to avoid, and — critically — helps you understand why those attempts failed before you propose something new.

finishTheLine.instructions: The salesperson has started a discovery question — but it's been cut off. Finish it in a way that opens up the conversation rather than closing it down. Use vocabulary and phrases from this lesson. Compare your versions, then click to see a suggested answer.

items.salespersonStart: When you say it's a mess — what does that
items.suggestedCompletion: look like in practice? Is it that the data isn't there, or that you have the data but no one trusts it or knows how to use it? I want to understand exactly where the breakdown is before I go any further.

items.customerLine: Prospect has just described three separate problems — slow approvals, manual reporting, and inconsistent follow-up.
items.salespersonStart: That's really helpful context. If you could change
items.suggestedCompletion: one thing about how the team operates right now — just one — which of those three would make the biggest difference to you? I want to make sure we focus on what actually matters most, not just what's loudest.

items.customerLine: Prospect: 'We've looked at a couple of solutions before but it never went anywhere.'
items.salespersonStart: I'd like to understand that better — what have you
items.suggestedCompletion: tried so far, and what happened? I'm not asking to be nosy — I just don't want to waste your time suggesting something that's already been on the table. Knowing what didn't work is as useful to me as knowing what you need.

items.salespersonStart: That's a clear goal. What would good
